mink.types: Mink is traded as pelts graded by sex, size, color, clarity and fur quality. Male pelts are larger with longer, coarser guard hair; female pelts are smaller, lighter and often finer, and garment makers choose between them for weight and drape. Farmed color types range from dark browns and blacks to paler mutation colors such as pastel and white, the product of generations of selective breeding. Pelts may be left natural, dyed, bleached, sheared to a velvety pile or plucked of guard hair. Construction also defines grade: full-skin garments, let-out garments in which pelts are cut into narrow diagonal strips and resewn to lengthen them, and cheaper pieced goods assembled from sections, paws or tails. Knitted mink uses narrow fur strips worked into a knit.
mink.fabrics: Mink is used as dressed skins rather than spun fiber. Full-length coats, jackets, stoles and capes are the traditional products, typically lined with silk or synthetic satin. Collars, cuffs and hood trims attach mink to wool or down outerwear, and pompoms and key chains use off-cuts. Sheared mink, trimmed to an even short pile, is used reversibly or with lighter linings. Knitted or woven mink cuts pelts into long thin strips that are knitted or woven with a yarn base, making lighter scarves and throws. Mink is also used in accessories such as hats, gloves and bag trims. Some cosmetic brushes and eyelash products have used mink hair, a separate market with its own labeling questions.
mink.quality: Quality shows in dense, even underfur that springs back when blown on, lustrous guard hairs of uniform length, and a soft, supple leather side that does not crackle. Tug gently: more than a few loose hairs suggests poor dressing or age. Matched color and seams that lie flat indicate careful construction; let-out work should show fine, even seams. Stiffness, odor, yellowing or tears in the leather indicate aging. In the US, the Fur Products Labeling Act requires labels to give the animal name, country of origin for imported fur, and whether the fur is dyed or bleached, pieced from paws, tails or bellies, or used. A missing or vague label is a red flag. Price depends heavily on construction and whether the pelts are whole.
pros: Dense underfur and guard hair give high warmth for weight and good wind resistance.
Well-dressed and stored mink garments can last many years and be remodeled.
The pelt surface sheds light rain and snow.
Mink is lighter and more supple than many longer-haired furs.
cons: Farming animals in cages raises welfare concerns that EFSA found could not be fully mitigated in current systems.
Sale and farming are restricted or banned in a growing number of jurisdictions.
It requires specialist cleaning and cool, ventilated storage.
Species and origin are hard for buyers to verify without documentation.
mink.impact: Mink impact debates center on animal welfare, disease and processing. The 2025 EFSA opinion found that key welfare consequences of cage systems could not be prevented within them, and experimental work shows farmed mink in non-enriched cages develop more stereotypic behavior, such as pacing, than those given enrichment. SARS-CoV-2 outbreaks on mink farms in 2020 showed how dense animal husbandry can create zoonotic risk. Environmentally, mink are carnivores fed on animal by-products, and pelts must be dressed and often dyed with chemical treatments; this review found no independent, peer-reviewed life cycle comparison of mink with faux fur, so claims on either side should be treated as contested. Legal context is shifting: California banned the sale of new fur products from 2023.
mink.care: Fur needs specialist care, and the label and a qualified furrier govern. Store mink on a broad, shaped hanger in a breathable cloth bag, never plastic, in a cool, dark, ventilated place; many owners use professional cold storage in warm months to protect against heat, humidity and insects. Keep it away from perfume, hairspray and shoulder-bag straps, which abrade and stain. If it gets wet, shake it out and hang it to dry at room temperature away from radiators; do not brush or use a hair dryer. Never iron, machine wash or home dry clean it. Have it professionally cleaned about once a year and small tears repaired promptly before they spread. Heat, light and dryness cause the leather to become brittle.
faq: How can I tell real mink from faux fur?

Part the hair at the base. Real fur grows from leather skin, while faux fur is attached to a knitted or woven fabric backing. Real hair tapers to a fine point and a singed hair smells of burnt hair, whereas acrylic faux fur melts. A label is required in the US for fur products.
Is it legal to sell mink in California?

Since 1 January 2023, California law (AB 44) has prohibited selling, offering, displaying for sale or manufacturing new fur products, with exceptions such as used or vintage fur, religious and tribal use, and certain species. Other jurisdictions have their own rules, so check the local law.
How long does a mink coat last?

With professional cleaning and proper cool storage, a mink coat can last for decades, and furriers can remodel or reline it. Heat, dryness and improper storage make the leather brittle and cause hair loss. Visible tears, stiffness or heavy shedding signal that the leather is deteriorating.

Letting out is a furrier technique in which each pelt is cut into narrow diagonal strips and sewn back together offset, making the skin longer and narrower. It creates long, flowing vertical lines in a coat and uses skilled labor, which is why let-out garments usually cost more than those made from whole or pieced skins.
notable: The US Truth in Fur Labeling Act of 2010 ended an exemption that had let fur items with less than $150 of fur go unlabeled.
Studies of farmed mink found that animals raised in barren cages show more stereotypic pacing and that enrichment reduces it.
California became the first US state to ban the sale and manufacture of new fur products, effective 1 January 2023.
